lines: This episode is about stance, and the body positions you can shoot from.
The book says the manner in which you stand is an important fundamental of shooting a firearm.

scenes.heading: The seven fundamentals
lines: The aim of Module 4 is to enable you to master the fundamentals of shooting.
Shooting is a skill, and each individual part of that skill must be mastered.

scenes.heading: Three body positions
lines: Three body positions can be adopted when shooting a firearm.
The situation you are faced with, and your environment, will dictate which body position you use.

scenes.definition: The body position used when firing the gun.
lines: The term stance refers to the body position used when firing the gun.
In other words, your stance will provide a secure platform from which the gun will be fired.

scenes.heading: The Isosceles Stance
scenes.caption: Front, side and top view of the Isosceles Stance
lines: The standing position is the fastest and most commonly used shooting position.
The recommended stance is called the Isosceles Stance.
It's called that because your legs and arms form two isosceles triangles.

scenes.heading: How to stand
bullets: Both arms straight out towards the target
A slight bend in your knees
Upper body bent very slightly forward

lines.text: Stand with your feet about shoulder width apart.
Thrust both arms straight out in front of you, towards the target.

lines: This stance allows you to develop a natural point of aim.
That means the gun will already be pointed at the target before you look at the sights.

lines.text: Now put a slight bend in your knees, to help with balance and to compensate for the recoil.
The top part of your body should be bent very slightly forward.

scenes.heading: Facing head-on
scenes.caption: Two shooters in the Isosceles Stance
lines: In the Isosceles Stance, you face your opponent head-on.
The book lists four advantages of this stance.

scenes.heading: Advantages of the Isosceles Stance
bullets: Head-on: full peripheral vision, both eyes
Bullet proof vest: no turning sideways

lines.text: One: you face your opponent head-on, so you have full use of your peripheral vision from both eyes.

lines: That gives you a wider field of vision, to see additional attackers or identify objects that can be used for cover.

lines.text: Two: this stance feeds off gross physical strength.

lines: So you won't be too badly affected by the adrenalin rush of using a firearm in a life threatening situation.

lines.text: Three: it provides a well-balanced platform, and allows fast movement in any direction.
Four: if you are wearing a bullet proof vest, this stance will prevent you from turning sideways.

lines: Turning sideways could get you shot in an area that the bullet proof vest does not protect.

scenes.heading: Weaver Stance
scenes.caption: Weaver Stance behind a barricade
lines: Next, the Weaver Stance.
Shooting sideways towards the target is the recommended stance to use when shooting from behind cover.
Notice how little of the shooter's body is visible to his opponent.
This stance allows you to remain hidden behind cover.

scenes.heading: The disadvantage
scenes.caption: Standing position: the bullet travels at shoulder height
lines: The disadvantage of this position is that if you miss your target, the bullet will be travelling at shoulder height.
That could endanger innocent bystanders.
If the shot misses, or passes straight through the attacker, bystanders in the background might be hit.

scenes.heading: Kneeling Position
scenes.caption: High kneeling and low kneeling positions
lines: The kneeling position is often used when you want to make yourself a smaller target to your opponent.
Or so you can stay hidden behind cover.
The high kneeling position is used for firing over objects being used as cover.
In the low kneeling position, the shooter is crouched low, to make himself a smaller target.

scenes.heading: Kneeling at close quarters
scenes.caption: Kneeling position: firing up, over the bystanders
lines: An advantage of the kneeling position, if used at close quarters, is that if you are firing up at your target, the bullet will travel over the heads of innocent bystanders.
If the attacker is missed, or the bullet passes through, the bystanders might not be harmed.
This can be a very safe and effective position if used when firing in crowded buildings.

rule.text: The prone position is used only as a last resort, because once you use it, you will not be able to move easily.
rule.label: Prone position

lines: Now, the prone position.
The prone position is used only as a last resort.
Because once you use the prone position, you will not be able to move easily.

scenes.heading: Standard Prone Position
scenes.caption: Standard prone position
lines: Here is the standard prone position.
It does have two advantages.

scenes.heading: Advantages of the prone position
bullets: Stable platform: accuracy over a long distance
A smaller target to your opponent
lines: It provides a stable platform, which will increase accuracy over a long distance.
And it makes you a smaller target to your opponent.

scenes.heading: Sideways Prone Position
scenes.caption: Sideways prone position
lines: The book also shows the sideways prone position.
This position can be used when lying behind cover.

scenes.heading: Supine Position
scenes.caption: Supine position
lines: And finally, the supine position.
It is most commonly used when the shooter has to fall backwards and fire from the supine position.

scenes.question: Which stance is recommended when shooting from behind cover?
lines: Here's a question from your formative exam.
Which stance is recommended when shooting from behind cover?
reveal: Shooting sideways towards the target is the recommended stance to use when shooting from behind cover.

scenes.question: In the Isosceles Stance, how far apart should your feet be?
lines: One more from the exam.
In the Isosceles Stance, how far apart should your feet be?
reveal: Then thrust both arms straight out in front of you, towards the target.

points: Isosceles: feet shoulder width, arms straight out
Kneeling: a smaller target, fire over bystanders
Prone: a last resort, you can't move easily
lines: So, there are seven fundamentals, and stance is the first.
The Isosceles Stance is the recommended stance, with feet shoulder width apart and both arms straight out.
The Weaver Stance is for shooting sideways from behind cover.
Kneeling makes you a smaller target, and firing up at close quarters sends the bullet over the heads of bystanders.
And prone is a last resort, because you will not be able to move easily.
